headline: A Kampala Developer Bets on Matchmaking for the Indie Founder Era
lede: When Nobert Patrick Wise, a full-stack developer based in Kampala, Uganda, posted that “you actually need real coding knowledge to vibe-code properly,” he was wading into one of the louder debates in developer culture. The follow-up in the same thread was a product pitch: ShipTogether, his own co-founder matching platform, built to connect founders, developers, and designers who want a build partner before they ship.
body:
ShipTogether (shiptogether.dev) is a mobile-first *co-founder matching* platform that borrows its UX liberally from dating apps: swipeable profile cards, mutual-match messaging, and an integrated scheduling feature for “coffee chats.” Users declare their skills and what kind of collaborator they need; the platform’s algorithm surfaces candidates. Wise, building under the Trikcode Technologies banner, launched the iOS app in November 2025 and has iterated to version 1.0.6. As of May 2026, it carries two App Store ratings and no significant press coverage — an early-stage product in every sense.

The market it enters is crowded and, so far, unconquered. Y Combinator’s co-founder matching service, free to all, claims over 100,000 matches made and 12,200 active profiles spread across San Francisco, New York, London, and Bangalore. CoFoundersLab has 650,000 registered users but a reputation for dead profiles and a cumbersome free tier. At least sixteen dedicated platforms jostle for the same niche without any one achieving the *network effect* that would make the choice obvious. Y Combinator’s own standing advice cuts against the category: “You’re much better off looking at the people you’ve worked with before.”

That advice exists because the underlying problem is severe. Harvard Business School professor Noam Wasserman, drawing on data from roughly 10,000 founders, found that **65% of high-potential startups fail due to conflict among co-founders** — a figure recited in virtually every accelerator curriculum. The root cause is rarely incompetence; it’s misalignment in values, motivations, and expectations that doesn’t surface until the company runs short of easy decisions. No matching algorithm has demonstrated it can reliably predict that kind of compatibility. Y Combinator notes 28 funded companies whose founders met through its platform — a meaningful signal, but not proof of concept at scale.

Wise’s aside about *vibe coding* — the term Andrej Karpathy coined in February 2025 to describe AI-assisted development where the programmer “fully gives in to the vibes” and stops reasoning closely about what the code does — adds a layer of irony. Engineers including Simon Willison, co-creator of the Django web framework, and AI researcher Andrew Ng have argued that vibe coding works precisely *because* its most prominent practitioners already know how to code: expertise is what makes AI-generated output safe to ship. A CodeRabbit analysis of 470 open-source pull requests found AI-co-authored code carried 1.7× more major issues and 2.74× more security vulnerabilities than human-written code. Wise, with a GitHub history spanning 119 repositories — AI tooling, database utilities, full-stack web — represents the profile critics have in mind when they argue skilled developers are doing something fundamentally different from true vibe coding: using AI as an accelerant, not a replacement.

concepts.definition: A style of AI-assisted programming, named by researcher Andrej Karpathy in February 2025, in which the developer delegates most code-writing to a large language model and accepts or rejects suggestions without closely reasoning about the underlying logic. Critics argue the approach is only safe when the practitioner already has enough expertise to detect when the AI’s output is wrong.

The practice of using a structured platform or program to pair solo founders with complementary collaborators — typically a technical co-founder seeking a business partner, or vice versa. Platforms range from free institutional tools to subscription marketplaces. Success rates are hard to measure because most matches never result in funded companies.

The phenomenon by which a platform becomes more valuable as more people join it, because each additional user enlarges the pool of potential matches or connections. Co-founder matching platforms depend on network effects to surface quality candidates, but few have achieved the critical mass needed to become the obvious first stop for solo founders.

fact_check: The poster frames the view that vibe coding requires real coding knowledge as an “unpopular opinion,” but credible engineers including Simon Willison and Andrew Ng have made essentially the same argument publicly, and it is increasingly mainstream among experienced practitioners. Calling it unpopular is at best a rhetorical move; the claim itself is well-supported.
thread_summary: @trikcode opened the thread with the argument that effective vibe coding demands genuine programming knowledge — an increasingly mainstream position despite the term’s casual origins. The bookmarked follow-up promoted ShipTogether, his own co-founder matching platform, pairing the philosophical claim (technical skills matter) with the product pitch (find a technically capable co-founder here).
